analysis.one_liner: Raises the evidence bar for federal civil asset seizures and ends agencies keeping the proceeds.
analysis.headline: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill in July 2014, but it never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died without a vote when Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Civil asset forfeiture lets the government take cash, cars, and other property suspected of being tied to a crime, often without charging the owner with anything. This bill would have forced the government to prove with clear and convincing evidence — a much higher bar than today's "more likely than not" standard — that the owner knowingly used the property or looked away from its criminal use. It would also have stopped the Justice Department from keeping the proceeds of forfeited property and sent that money to the Treasury's general fund instead, so the agencies doing the seizing no longer profit directly from it.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of cash, cars, homes, and businesses seized under federal civil forfeiture law — including people never charged with a crime — would face a government that has to prove far more to keep their property and that no longer profits directly from taking it. Taxpayers would receive the proceeds through the Treasury's general fund rather than through agency budgets.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's standard of proof in federal civil forfeiture cases from 'a preponderance of the evidence' — barely more likely than not — to 'clear and convincing evidence.'

Requires the government to prove the owner intentionally used the property in the offense, knowingly consented to it, or was willfully blind to it, rather than just showing the property had some connection to a crime.

Ends the practice of depositing forfeiture proceeds into Department of Justice accounts that fund law enforcement; the money would go to the Treasury's General Fund instead, removing the agency's direct financial stake in seizures.
Applies to civil forfeiture proceedings already pending when the bill took effect, so owners fighting seizures at the time would get the new protections.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies would lose the forfeiture revenue that currently funds their activities through DOJ accounts, and state and local agencies that share in federal seizures would see less of that money. Prosecutors would face a heavier evidentiary burden in every civil forfeiture case.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies funded by seizures

drawbacks.text: The higher standard and the owner-fault requirement would make it harder for prosecutors to forfeit assets connected to crime, including property of organizations whose owners claim not to know about the criminal use.

Agencies that currently fund training, equipment, and other law enforcement activities from forfeiture proceeds would lose that money and would have to seek regular congressional appropriations instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: today a person can lose cash, a car, or a home without ever being charged with a crime, because the government only has to show it is slightly more likely than not that the property was connected to an offense, and the agency that seized the property keeps the money. This bill would have raised the evidentiary bar, required proof the owner was knowingly involved, and cut the financial reward for seizing — attacking the incentive problem directly. The honest cost: prosecutors would have a harder time stripping assets from criminal enterprises, especially where owners claim ignorance, and agencies would lose a funding stream they currently use for operations. That loss of funding was partly the point — removing the incentive to seize for profit — but it is a real cost to law enforcement capability and would have required new appropriations to replace.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Paul introduced the bill and the Senate Judiciary Committee never took it up, so it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the FAIR Act on July 23, 2014; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
That referral was the bill's last action of record: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever happened.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies keep the current system, in which they can seize property with a low burden of proof and keep the proceeds for their own activities. Property owners gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies; property owners got nothing

for.name: Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act on July 23, 2014 and pushed it as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Angus King
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator to join Paul.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators supported the bill — a Republican sponsor and an Independent cosponsor (S4) — and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split appears in the record; it died in a committee controlled by the other party.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (DOJ Assets Forfeiture Fund)
industries.note: Under current law the Justice Department keeps proceeds from forfeited property in accounts that fund law enforcement activities. The bill would send that money to the Treasury General Fund instead, cutting the department's direct financial stake in seizures.

industries.industry: State and local police departments that share federal forfeiture proceeds
industries.note: Federal forfeiture money flows to state and local agencies that assist federal seizures. Redirecting proceeds to the Treasury would shrink that stream and weaken the financial incentive for police to join in taking property for revenue.
